posts.name: Tomb
posts.cooked:
A few points i wanted to go into just to share what i’ve learned and my experiences with Arenas and how these ranked type games work. I’m going to build a timeline of how the arena ceiling is created and why I just couldn’t compete. It was way worse than I realized. I just want to state… that I quit arenas A LONG TIME AGO. Not in tbc. I’m talking mysts of pandaria.

  1. A new expansion drops
  • The best arena players know this: Rush to max level. Do whatever it takes. They do this because
    a. it creates a pvp gearing advantage. They will min max all their gear.
    b. they are testing out pvp before you even hit max level
    c. by the time I hit max level, they’ve got 5,000 arena games behind them
    d. they already have multiple alts

-This starts to create a ceiling What is the ceiling? An approximate arena ranking of x amount. At this point it’s probably low. It’s early in Arena season 1. The best players in the world are competing with each other and slowly climbing in rating. These people are playing way more than me. The higher IQ players climb faster.

  1. They level more alts
  • They level alts of every class. Whatever is the meta at the time they push with that. The ceiling starts dropping even more. These players are playing with the same people they already play with. They are best friends. They gear up, they test things. You run into elite arena players in 1500 rankings gearing up alts. They push to 1600, 1700, 1800, way faster than you. They dominate 2200+… THEY MAY HAVE 10 ALTS ABOVE 2K… creates a ceiling. That means! Theoretically the top 200 arenas players could possibly be the top 2000 characters in the ranking system. The wow boosting system… allows this to proliferate even further.
  1. They play way more than you.
  • Some people are more casual… they come in and meet the minimum requirements to get their points for the week. They stop. Some people get frustrated 3 or 4 games in and say “screw this I’m going raid kara”. Some people have limited time and have social life, and try to squeeze in as many games as they can. The top 200 players are serious… they play 12-14 hours a day. The chance of me encountering these people are much higher than me encountering a “semi-casual” player. The higher your ranking is, the more likely you will run into a top 200 player. Because they are constantly leveling new alts.
  1. They have way more knowledge of the game than you.
  • I’m still trying to learn holy paladin… They know every class and every spec. They know how a mage is setting up for burst… they know how long a rogue can stun lock you out. They know that your warlock, just blew all their cooldowns. They coming in hard. They know all they have to do now is just cc you, because you have no defensives left. They know the weaknesses and strengths of every comp. They’ve already experimented 5 different ways to beat you out. They aren’t just thinking “oh all we have to do is get a cc lock on them”. They are playing 5 different strategies simultaneously to wear you down. They laugh because of how easy it is to beat me.

  1. Elite players accumulate social capital. A casual player may have to find random teammates sometimes and repeatedly rebuild coordination. Established arena players know the same people who’ve been playing for years.

  2. The ladder expands underneath the early hardcore arena population. Initially in arena season 1 the best players initially fight mostly one another but as tens of thousands of less-experienced players arrive, their ratings increase.

You every experience a night where it’s just like “man these people at my rating are playing like professionals!!”? Ya, because you were.

  1. The rating distribution. Look at the distribution for TBC, the Top 20 teams have a delta of 124 arena points. The next 20 characters drop 28. So yea you may be thinking “dude i’m only 50 points away from a 2k rating”… but you are approaching a cliff in the distribution. Each additional rating point is asking you to move past players in an exponential fashion. And remember, those are characters, not unique people. So the pyramid isn’t even a pyramid it’s a concave sided pyramid… with dramatic differences every 100 points. At 1900 in tbc the difference in 20 players is only 4 points. The compression above 1900 is enormous. That’s basically a traffic jam. So at 200th place you’re only at 1844. So i took all that data and plugged it into chatgpt.
  • characters above 2k - 49
  • characters above 1900 - 162
  • characters above 1800 - 407
  • characters above 1700 - 969
  • chacters above 1600 - 2006
  • characters above 1500 - 4400

Here’s another interesting data point.
21.7% of players above 1900 never played more than 50 games. How did they get that high with only playing 50 games? They moved through the ladder VERY efficiently. They arrived already capable of winning at a high rate. It’s questionable isn’t it? How does one get that high of a rating with only playing 50 games in one season? The rating resets at beginning of season, there’s a structural advantage. He arrived prepared, shot through the distribution, and parked the character. They hit the rating they care about at the beginning of the season, and then park. They stop playing games.

There’s a few grinders here. Theres a lock at 1711 with 202 games. A rogue at 1736 with 159 games. Other players have nowhere near the amount of games they have.

95% of this siampled ladder has fewer than 100 games.

So you end up with a distribution that looks like 160 characters above 1900. While most of the characters are never actually queuing regularly. Then the next wave of elite players comes through with Alts, and they park. What does that mean? These players are constantly playing in middle and lower ladder levels.

Meaningful games above 1800? Very little. The continuously population above 1800 is actually very small. What does that tell you? 2100 - 1800 IS FAKE!!!

THAT MEANS… THE TOP PLAYERS ARE PLAYING IN THE 1700 RANKINGS!!! 563 characters from 1700-1800. Let’s say they each have 6 alts. THE BEST PLAYERS IN THE WORLD ARE A GROUP OF ABOUT 100 PEOPLE.

With the SCARY IMPLICATION OF THE COMPRESSION MODEL you are competing against the best players in the world at 1600 to 1700 rankings. It’s easy to lose two games and drop 50 points…

You’re not as bad as they want you to think.

I started in Arena season 2. Trying to get that weapon, but i was too much of a noob. I was clicking all my abilities up until about… cata. Why? because i had no idea what keybinding even was. I was a noob that sucked at the game but that carrot kept me there. Still in wotlk, barely broke 1800. It was harder then. These were 2v2s. I sucked even worse in 3v3s. By the time i hit max level in cata i entered arenas and was getting 2 shotted by warlocks. I skipped out cata, was mad a blizzard for taking my auras and professions. Started playing SC2, a guy showed me what keybindings are. Came back in MOP with keybindings and made it to 1950. Got a Rival achievement or something. Which was like top 10% or something ya know. I was proud of that and I should have been. Almost dropped out of college that year… I’d miss 2 weeks of class straight and my professors would be like “where ya been dude??!”. I had to come up with some excuse.. told them i had pink eye. They said “FOR TWO WEEKS?”. I said yea it was really bad. They thought i was addicted to hard drugs or something. I wasn’t. I was just grinding arenas 12 hours a day LOL.

I decided after MOP that I wasn’t going to chase that train anymore. Played a little in WOD and a little in Legion. Messed around with a resto druid. Did pretty well. Never broke 2k. Classic came out… quit retail forever. I was only playing retail for pvp. I had a lot of fun raiding with my freinds in wotlk. They all left. The serious players transferred off our Boulderfist server to some mega giant server. We lost all our top dps. By MOP there was one raiding guild left on the server. I played with them, but they already had an established team. There was politics involved. I grew resentful. Eventually I just became a solo player… drifting around on random arena teams. There was nothing tying me to the game.

What you dont know about arena ranking is that because now they’re using PR instead of team rating you can really cheese the thing easily.

At every bracket there are comps that shine above others in that rating range, I would spell it out but for the sake of saving space, just be aware that different comps are dominant at different levels of play and because of this you can build counter comps VS those “dominant” comps, this allows you to basically comp swap on the way up.

The way the Modern MMR system works is that it will attempt to find the “Rating” where it thinks you belong, and as a result if you don’t have any losses or very little you raise in Rating much faster.

The way MMR works now days VS how it worked PRE-OG-WoD is a massively different system that is designed to force a grind..

If you go back to OG TBC, Wrath, Cata, and MoP you could go from Zero to around 2200 in under 20 games /played even wtih a couple of losses, but this required way better play because you’re not able to team hop due to it being a Team based game not a personal rating scam.

Hope that makes sense.

Point being arena is fun, but it has never been “balanced”, its had moments where it got close like 5.2/5.3 mop, but its so short lived that its not even worth mentioning when for the bulk of arena’s existence its been designed on the idea that if you want to win then you are suppose to play the meta comp(s) depending on the expansion / patch you are in example being like playing RMP in 3’s for TBC.

Arena is a nice idea that dies the moment people figure out that blizzard is picking the winners before the game starts.

posts.name: Lazarus
posts.cooked:
It’s good you have the self awareness to understand your limitations.

MMORPGs tend to have the problem of ‘gear mattering’ with time and progression and something like a supposed skill metric based match rating system. This has always been a flaw in arena where it was supposed to be skill mattering, not anything else like gear. Then there’s other issues with arena like class composition balance and ‘who you know’. There’s 1 spot for 'the best player of X class/spec" and anyone else who doesn’t know them is at a bigger deficit. This isn’t even considering things like player synergy.

I’d say a better example of a MMR rating being more equivalent to skill, (still has problems) is league of legends with solo queue. It still has problems of not being a 1v1, (so your teammates will always have a influence) but it does have a higher skill cap due to more teammates & opponents to track than 1v1. League of Legends is a good example of how human talent distribution and variables can show up. Some people are young and have a lot of time. Some once did, but not so much anymore (busy with work/college and not just having AI/someone else do it) some people have some good things they do sometimes, (Kadeem) but overall are missing too much of the piece of the puzzle, so a lot of ‘how they play and practice’ is wrong and isn’t good training. There’s some really smart players that play these games whether it’s vanilla pvp or League, but they also have their own desires with their talents and own real life obligations or what have you. Around Season 3 & 4 in League of Legends most everyone was looking down on the South Koreans because “NA was the best” given Season 1 and 2, then the people who were looking at season 3 were largely mocked or shrugged off. That ushered in the era of South Korean and European supremacy when they had the best players. NA has since become not as much NA anymore because a lot of those players in those teams came from other regions, e.g. Bjergsen from EU.

Season 3 had heavy hitters like Apdo who would sell accounts/boost in the South Korean ladder. Apdo was a Zed main and was said to be the best or one of the best Zed players before Faker or Dade. Apdo didn’t seem to have much interest in being a pro player, he’d rather do things on his own time and make money selling stuff in ranked.

Our own NA ladder has similar people who can be very gifted but get obligated with other stuff. Some people are just really talented at things or fast learners. You ever see Bob Munden shoot a revolver at two targets feet away faster than anyone can blink or react? It’s insane. That’s not “a skill that anyone can learn with 10k” hours"

Regardless, history and human experience shows the ‘10k hours and be a master’ is not a true idiom. Even if a lot of people, or any two people, were given good consistent hours of good quality training, there’s little reason to expect them to be exactly as talented and skillful as each other. Inequality, disparity and chaos is the natural state of the world.

I won’t belabor this thread with the argument of whether talent exists or to what extent or whether ‘everyone is just as smart and talented and has just as much potential’ much past this.

It’s enough to say that some players like Kadeem can spend more than 10k hours playing League, and others will have some form of game smarts that propel them towards much higher ranks and they can consistently get those high ranks even on ‘smurf’ accounts, (related to OP, this does muck up the integrity of the rating and skill system) instead of the person who got lucky and can’t perform when asked to again.

Vanilla WoW is a deceptively high skill game. Arenas still has quite a bit of skill when they’re not gaming the system like Steeldust said. Perplexity pulled up a warlock player with 2.8k+ rating or something on stream once and he noted how all he did was queue snipe into favorable matchups. “Oh, but he has 2.8k rating, he must be really good!” arena rating is not synonymous with skill. But there is a lot of skill in it whenever it’s done right. The amount of flow chart and RNG/response/mixups that players like Mir do and know and have ingrained in them is not something everyone is going to be equally skilled at even if they had the drive and time.

For players like Eastcoast or others who keep saying vanilla pvp is not complex or difficult, they always use a reductionist argument and time and time again fail to deliver results that should be easy according to them. That’s even worse, because it’s a unskillful game, and they can’t even deliver on that.
